                                  13          Before the Court are two administrative motions:
                                  14          (1) Google LLC’s (“Google”) Administrative Motion to File Under Seal. ECF No. 230.
                                  15          (2) Google’s Administrative Motion to Consider Whether Point Financial, Inc.’s (“PFI”)
                                  16              Material Should be Sealed. ECF No. 231.
                                  17          For the reasons set forth below, Google’s administrative motions are GRANTED to the
                                  18   extent Google requests redactions.
                                  19     I.   LEGAL STANDARD
                                  20          “Historically, courts have recognized a ‘general right to inspect and copy public records
                                  21   and documents, including judicial records and documents.’” Kamakana v. City & Cnty. of
                                  22   Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172, 1178 (9th Cir. 2006) (quoting Nixon v. Warner Commc’ns, Inc., 435
                                  23   U.S. 589, 597 & n.7 (1978)). Accordingly, when considering a sealing request, “a ‘strong
                                  24   presumption in favor of access’ is the starting point.” Id. (quoting Foltz v. State Farm Mut. Auto.
                                  25   Ins. Co., 331 F.3d 1122, 1135 (9th Cir. 2003)). Parties seeking to seal judicial records relating to
                                  26   motions that are “more than tangentially related to the underlying cause of action” bear the burden
                                  27   of overcoming the presumption with “compelling reasons” that outweigh the general history of
                                  28   access and the public policies favoring disclosure. Ctr. for Auto Safety v. Chrysler Grp., 809 F.3d
                                        Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF            Document 248           Filed 04/29/26      Page 2 of 19




                                   1   1092, 1099–101 (9th Cir. 2016); Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178–80.

                                   2           In addition, in this district, all parties requesting sealing must comply with Civil Local

                                   3   Rule 79-5. That rule requires, inter alia, the moving party to provide “the reasons for keeping a

                                   4   document under seal, including an explanation of: (i) the legitimate private or public interests that

                                   5   warrant sealing; (ii) the injury that will result if sealing is denied; and (iii) why a less restrictive

                                   6   alternative to sealing is not sufficient.” Civil L.R. 79-5(c)(1). Civil Local Rule 79-5 requires the

                                   7   moving party to provide “evidentiary support from declarations where necessary.” Civil L.R. 79-

                                   8   5(c)(2). And the proposed order must be “narrowly tailored to seal only the sealable material.”

                                   9   Civil L.R. 79-5(c)(3).

                                  10           Further, when a party seeks to seal a document because it has been designated as

                                  11   confidential by another party, the filing party must file an Administrative Motion to Consider

                                  12   Whether Another Party’s Material Should be Sealed. Civil L.R. 79-5(f). In that case, the filing
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   party need not satisfy the requirements of subsection (c)(1). Civil L.R. 79-5(f)(1). Instead, the

                                  14   party who designated the material as confidential must, within seven days of the motion’s filing,

                                  15   file a statement and/or declaration that meets the requirements of subsection (c)(1). Civil L.R. 79-

                                  16   5(f)(3). A designating party’s failure to file a statement or declaration may result in the unsealing

                                  17   of the provisionally sealed document without further notice to the designating party. Id. Any

                                  18   party can file a response to that declaration within four days. Civil L.R. 79-5(f)(4).

                                  19
                                        II.    ECF NO. 230
                                  20
                                               Google has filed an administrative motion to seal portions of its motion for partial
                                  21
                                       summary judgment and exhibits thereto. ECF No. 230. PFI opposes on the ground that the
                                  22
                                       “information Google seeks to seal has already been disclosed, is commonly known, and [is]
                                  23
                                       publicly available.” ECF No. 235 at 1.
                                  24
                                               Google separates its sealing requests into three categories. The first category is “terms,
                                  25
                                       phrases, and documents pertaining to Google’s confidential and proprietary technology at issue in
                                  26
                                       this litigation.” ECF No. 230 at 3. Google contends the disclosure of this information would
                                  27
                                       reveal Google’s confidential technology and in turn “weaken the competitive advantage Google
                                  28
                                                                                            2
                                        Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF           Document 248          Filed 04/29/26     Page 3 of 19




                                   1   maintains in the marketplace.” Id. The second category of requests consists of “confidential

                                   2   contracts with third parties” pertaining to Google’s plans to develop, design, and manufacture the

                                   3   chip at issue in this litigation. Id. Google argues that the disclosure of this information would

                                   4   expose Google’s “strategic decision-making with respect to the terms offered to its contracting

                                   5   partners” and, in turn, harm its competitive advantage. Id. The third category of information

                                   6   Google seeks to seal is non-public information pertaining to Google’s agreements with third

                                   7   parties and the identities of the vendors that manufacture, test, and assemble the at-issue chip. Id.

                                   8   at 3–4. According to Google, the public disclosure of this information would reveal Google’s

                                   9   strategy with respect to its contractual relationships and weaken its leverage. Id. at 4.

                                  10          As the sealing request relates to a motion for partial summary judgment, which the Court

                                  11   finds is “more than tangentially related to the underlying cause[s] of action,” the Court will apply

                                  12   the “compelling reasons” standard. Ctr. for Auto Safety, 809 F.3d at 1099–101. It may be, as PFI
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   argues, that some of the information Google seeks to seal is publicly known. See ECF No. 235

                                  14   at 1–4. But Google’s litigation documents aggregate confidential information in a single place,

                                  15   which heightens their sensitivity. The Court thus finds that compelling reasons exist to seal the

                                  16   materials Google identifies, because the “compelling reasons” standard is met for confidential

                                  17   business information that would harm a party’s competitive standing if publicly disclosed. See

                                  18   Music Grp. Macao Com. Offshore Ltd. v. Foote, No. 14-cv-03078, 2015 WL 3993147, at *6

                                  19   (N.D. Cal. June 30, 2015); Jam Cellars, Inc. v. Wine Grp. LLC, No. 19-cv-01878, 2020 WL

                                  20   5576346, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 17, 2020) (finding compelling reasons for sealing “confidential

                                  21   business and proprietary information”); Fed. Trade Comm’n v. Qualcomm Inc., No. 17-cv-00220,

                                  22   2019 WL 95922, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 3, 2019) (finding compelling reasons for sealing

                                  23   “information that, if published, may harm . . . competitive standing and divulges terms of

                                  24   confidential contracts, contract negotiations, or trade secrets”); In re Elec. Arts, Inc., 298 F. App’x

                                  25   568, 569 (9th Cir. 2008) (finding sealable “business information that might harm a litigant’s

                                  26   competitive standing”).

                                  27          The Court also finds that the request is narrowly tailored. See Civil L.R. 79-5(c)(3). The

                                  13          Before the Court are two administrative motions:
                                  14          (1) Point Financial, Inc.’s (“PFI”) Administrative Motion to Consider Whether PFI’s
                                  15              Motion for Summary Judgment and Supporting Exhibits Should Be Sealed. ECF
                                  16              No. 228.
                                  17          (2) Point Financial, Inc.’s (“PFI”) Administrative Motion to Consider Whether PFI’s
                                  18              Motion for Summary Judgment as Further Redacted and Supporting Exhibits Should
                                  19              Be Sealed. ECF No. 240.
                                  20          For the reasons set forth below, PFI’s administrative motions are GRANTED to the extent
                                  21   Google LLC (“Google”) seeks redactions.
                                  22     I.   LEGAL STANDARD
                                  23          “Historically, courts have recognized a ‘general right to inspect and copy public records
                                  24   and documents, including judicial records and documents.’” Kamakana v. City & Cnty. of
                                  25   Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172, 1178 (9th Cir. 2006) (quoting Nixon v. Warner Commc’ns, Inc., 435
                                  26   U.S. 589, 597 & n.7 (1978)). Accordingly, when considering a sealing request, “a ‘strong
                                  27   presumption in favor of access’ is the starting point.” Id. (quoting Foltz v. State Farm Mut. Auto.
                                  28   Ins. Co., 331 F.3d 1122, 1135 (9th Cir. 2003)). Parties seeking to seal judicial records relating to
                                         Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF            Document 247          Filed 04/28/26      Page 2 of 9




                                   1   motions that are “more than tangentially related to the underlying cause of action” bear the burden

                                   2   of overcoming the presumption with “compelling reasons” that outweigh the general history of

                                   3   access and the public policies favoring disclosure. Ctr. for Auto Safety v. Chrysler Grp., 809 F.3d

                                   4   1092, 1099–101 (9th Cir. 2016); Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178–80.

                                   5           In addition, in this district, all parties requesting sealing must comply with Civil Local

                                   6   Rule 79-5. That rule requires, inter alia, the moving party to provide “the reasons for keeping a

                                   7   document under seal, including an explanation of: (i) the legitimate private or public interests that

                                   8   warrant sealing; (ii) the injury that will result if sealing is denied; and (iii) why a less restrictive

                                   9   alternative to sealing is not sufficient.” Civil L.R. 79-5(c)(1). Civil Local Rule 79-5 requires the

                                  10   moving party to provide “evidentiary support from declarations where necessary.” Civil L.R. 79-

                                  11   5(c)(2). And the proposed order must be “narrowly tailored to seal only the sealable material.”

                                  12   Civil L.R. 79-5(c)(3).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           Further, when a party seeks to seal a document because it has been designated as

                                  14   confidential by another party, the filing party must file an Administrative Motion to Consider

                                  15   Whether Another Party’s Material Should be Sealed. Civil L.R. 79-5(f). In that case, the filing

                                  16   party need not satisfy the requirements of subsection (c)(1). Civil L.R. 79-5(f)(1). Instead, the

                                  17   party who designated the material as confidential must, within seven days of the motion’s filing,

                                  18   file a statement and/or declaration that meets the requirements of subsection (c)(1). Civil L.R. 79-

                                  19   5(f)(3). A designating party’s failure to file a statement or declaration may result in the unsealing

                                  20   of the provisionally sealed document without further notice to the designating party. Id. Any

                                  21   party can file a response to that declaration within four days. Civil L.R. 79-5(f)(4).

                                  22    II.    DISCUSSION
                                  23           PFI initially filed a motion for summary judgment, ECF No. 227, and an accompanying

                                  24   administrative motion to consider whether PFI’s motion for summary judgment and supporting

                                  25   exhibits should be sealed, ECF No. 228. PFI subsequently filed a motion to remove ECF No. 227

                                  26   from the docket, ECF No. 241, which the Court granted, ECF No. 242. As a consequence, PFI’s

                                  27   motion for summary judgment and all exhibits attached thereto have been removed from the

                                  28   docket. PFI then filed its corrected motion for summary judgment, ECF No. 239, and filed an
                                                                                            2
                                         Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF             Document 247         Filed 04/28/26      Page 3 of 9




                                   1   accompanying administrative motion to consider whether its motion for summary judgment as

                                   2   further redacted and supporting exhibits should be sealed, ECF No. 240.

                                   3             As an initial matter, the Court notes that there are no public versions of the exhibits to the

                                   4   motion for summary judgment on the docket, because the Court granted PFI’s motion to remove

                                   5   ECF No. 227. Accordingly, PFI is ORDERED to upload a complete public version of its motion

                                   6   for summary judgment, including exhibits that are entirely sealed (which should be identified with

                                   7   a placeholder page), exhibits with redactions, and exhibits that are not sealed at all. The Court

                                   8   requests that the exhibits be submitted in order (A-JJ) and be clearly labeled and identified on the

                                   9   docket.

                                  10             Turning to PFI’s administrative motions, Google filed statements in support of sealing.

                                  11   See ECF Nos. 237, 243. PFI did not file oppositions. Because Google’s statements in support of

                                  12   sealing are “substantively identical” with the exception of an additional requested redaction on
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   page 30 of Exhibit K, ECF No. 243 at 1, the Court analyzes the administrative motions together.

                                  14             Google separates its sealing requests into three categories. The first category is “terms,

                                  15   phrases, and documents pertaining to Google’s confidential and proprietary technology at issue in

                                  16   this litigation.” Id. at 2. Google contends the disclosure of this information would reveal

                                  17   Google’s confidential technology and in turn “weaken the competitive advantage Google

                                  18   maintains in the marketplace.” Id. at 2–3. The second category of requests consists of

                                  19   “confidential contracts with third parties” pertaining to Google’s plans to develop, design, and

                                  20   manufacture the chip at issue in this litigation. Id. at 3. Google argues that the disclosure of this
